blocks.en: Abstract
blocks.zh: 摘要

blocks.en: Learning humanoid loco-manipulation from human demonstrations rests on observing how locomotion, posture, and object interaction evolve together as tasks unfold. Scaling collection across diverse environments, in turn, favors lightweight, portable capture systems. Yet, existing datasets provide only partial views of this coordination. Thus, we introduce EgoExplorer, a 100-hour vision-motion-touch observatory of human loco-manipulation built with a wearable system. With an emphasis on professional activities, its continuous recordings align egocentric video with reconstructed whole-body motion, fine-grained finger articulation, and tactile observations, accompanied by step-level descriptions. To achieve this coverage with sparse body sensing, we develop the Calibrate-Complete-Constrain pipeline. Concretely, reusable calibration fixes participant geometry and sensor attachments before motion inference to disentangle mounting offsets from articulation. A temporal prior then completes unobserved joint motion, while layered constraints promote measurement agreement, temporal continuity, and geometric consistency, properties that motion plausibility alone does not guarantee. Against tracker-fitted references, the method reduces body-point error by 71.9% relative to the strongest baseline; matched evaluations also show gains in hand stability and contact estimation. Preliminary studies explore multimodal generation and conditioning alongside humanoid retargeting with whole-body control in simulation.

blocks.en:
What a humanoid needs to reach, grasp, or carry shapes where it moves and how it positions its body ( Shi et al., 2026 ) .
Learning such loco-manipulation skills calls for demonstrations spanning diverse environments, objects, and task sequences.
Robot teleoperation provides such
data, but dedicated hardware, on-site deployment, and sustained operator
effort constrain its scalability ( Zhu et al., 2026 ; Punamiya et al., 2026 ) .
Human activity offers a rich alternative across everyday and professional
settings, and recent work shows that egocentric demonstrations can improve
robot manipulation and generalization to novel scenarios ( Kareer et al., 2025 ; Qiu et al., 2025 ; Shi et al., 2026 ) .
Realizing this potential for loco-manipulation hinges on datasets that jointly record visual context, whole-body and hand motion, and measured contact throughout continuous tasks.

Building such datasets at scale entails balancing environmental coverage with the richness and fidelity of the observations.
Systems built around fixed camera arrays for optical motion
capture ( Cao et al., 2026 ) or multi-view reconstruction ( Bhatnagar et al., 2022 ; Zhang et al., 2022 ) can provide detailed observations, but
require each recording space to be instrumented and calibrated ( Taheri et al., 2020 ; Kim et al., 2025 ) . Portable capture eases deployment,
yet existing datasets often offer only partial views of this coordination.
Particularly, egocentric video preserves diverse visual context but leaves much of the
body unobserved ( Grauman et al., 2022 ) .
Wearable body tracking adds body motion, often without fine finger
articulation or physical contact measurements ( Ma et al., 2024 ; DeTone et al., 2026 ) .
Conversely, hand-focused datasets capture detailed hand motion and, in some cases
touch, but typically omit the accompanying whole-body movement ( Hoque et al., 2026 ; Zhou et al., 2026 ; Song et al., 2025 ) .
These partial records obscure the coupling central to loco-manipulation and therefore fall short of capturing its execution as a coherent whole.

To this end, we introduce EgoExplorer , an egocentric dataset that captures the whole-body
coordination underlying human loco-manipulation through portable
vision-motion-touch sensing.
As depicted in Fig. 1 , it aligns first-person video with
reconstructed body motion, glove-measured finger articulation, and tactile
observations. Collected across five environments with an emphasis on professional activities, the recordings preserve the transitions between approaching targets, adjusting posture, manipulating objects, and relocating.
Step-level descriptions link these synchronized observations to the actions and progression of each task.

blocks.en:
To support this multimodal capture, our lightweight wearable rig combines five trackers, instrumented gloves, and a head-mounted camera.
Recovering whole-body trajectories requires inferring unobserved joint motion from these sparse device poses.
Yet direct fitting is ambiguous: each pose depends jointly on its attachment transform and the body’s kinematic chain, allowing different combinations of mounting offsets and joint configurations to explain the same sparse measurements ( Jiang et al., 2022 ; Ponton et al., 2023 ) .
Differently, our C 3 \mathrm{C}^{3} pipeline ( Calibrate-Complete-Constrain ) disentangles fixed body-sensor geometry from motion through a calibration protocol: prescribed participant movements are matched to a reference motion library.
Using these correspondences, we refine initial estimates of body shape and scale and fit body-sensor transforms, forming a profile reusable across tasks with unchanged sensor placement.
A temporal prior model then completes unobserved articulation from the calibrated anchors, yielding an initial whole-body trajectory, i.e. , the motion proposal.
We refine this proposal under layered constraints to promote measurement agreement and temporal continuity while penalizing self-interpenetration and ground penetration.
Finally, we incorporate hand motion, touch, and expert-guided step annotations and check multimodal consistency.
The resulting dataset comprises 2,715 egocentric recordings totaling 100 hours ( Tab. 1 ).

We evaluate annotation accuracy on a purpose-built Evaluation Subset and
reconstruction consistency on the Natural Recordings. Compared with the strongest
evaluated body-reconstruction baseline, our system reduces body-point error
by 71.9%. Hand and contact tests also show better holding stability,
kinematic target recovery, and regional contact estimation than the evaluated
alternatives, supporting the benefits of calibrated reconstruction and
direct hand sensing.
Beyond annotation quality, we conduct a preliminary exploration of training
utility through Cosmos-based ( NVIDIA, 2026 ) multimodal prediction
and human-to-robot motion transfer using ZeroWBC-style ( Yang et al., 2026a ) whole-body control in simulation. These initial studies suggest
benefits from combining synchronized modalities and illustrate the potential
of the recordings for policy learning.

blocks.en: We summarize our contributions as follows: (i) EgoExplorer , a vision-motion-touch dataset that achieves rich multimodal coverage and high-fidelity motion annotations with lightweight instrumentation, capturing continuous human loco-manipulation; (ii) the C 3 \mathrm{C}^{3} pipeline, which decouples body-sensor calibration from motion inference and combines temporal completion with layered constraints to recover metric whole-body motion from sparse trackers. (iii) experiments demonstrating improved annotation quality and the effectiveness of our design choices, complemented by an initial assessment of the recordings’ utility for embodied learning.

and camera motion ( Shen et al., 2024 ; Zhang et al., 2025 ; Xu et al., 2026 ) .

motion completion, and constrained refinement to address sensor mismatch, self-intersection, and floor penetration.

blocks.en: 3 The EgoExplorer Dataset
blocks.zh: 3 电子爆炸数据集

blocks.en:
Egocentric video captures task semantics at scale, yet leaves key signals for loco-manipulation under-constrained: hand articulation is obscured;
whole-body motion, especially lower-body support, extends beyond the camera’s field of view; and appearance alone cannot reveal tactile contact. EgoExplorer addresses this asymmetry by pairing a head-mounted camera with sparse wearable sensing, grounding body and hand motion in sensor measurements and corresponding touch records.
The dataset contains 2,715 recordings (100 h) across ten task templates and five environments, spanning laboratories, factories, and homes.
Following the workflow in Fig. 2 , we first introduce the capture hardware ( Sec. 3.1 ), then describe sensor calibration, body completion, and constrained refinement of fine-grained body reconstruction ( Sec. 3.2 ), and enrich the episodes with expert-guided task boundaries and annotations ( Sec. 3.3 ). Sec. 4 offers a glimpse of the dataset.

blocks.en: 3.1 Capture Hardware
blocks.zh: 3.1 抓取硬件

blocks.en:
Requirements. Fine-grained loco-manipulation capture requires accurate measurements of body motion, hand articulation, and contact in a lightweight, portable system.
Studio motion capture ( Taheri et al., 2020 ; Kim et al., 2025 ; Cao et al., 2026 ) provides dense measurements but confines collection to a calibrated multi-camera volume, whereas readily deployable video-only capture ( Shen et al., 2024 ; Zhang et al., 2025 ) must infer occluded motion and visually ambiguous contact.
We therefore complement sparse tracking at key body joints with direct finger sensing and optional touch for whole-body reconstruction and fine-grained interaction annotation.
blocks.zh:
所需经费。 精细的光线操纵活性捕捉需要精确地测量身体运动,手语,和在轻量级,便携式系统中的接触.
工作室运动捕捉(Taheri等,2020年;Kim等,2025年;Cao等,2026年)提供密集的测量,但将采集限制在可校准的多相机体积上,而随时可部署的仅录相机捕捉(Shen等,2024年;Zhang等,2025年)则必须推断出运动被隐蔽和视似模糊的接触.
因此,我们用直接指感和可选触来补充关键身体关节的零星跟踪,用于全身重建以及精细的相互作用说明。

blocks.en:
Hardware. Five VIVE Ultimate Trackers locate the head, hands, and ankles ( App. A ), using onboard cameras for 6-DoF inside-out tracking without external base stations.
Head and hand trackers establish metric camera and end-effector trajectories, while ankle trackers capture foot placement and constrain stance and support beyond the head camera’s view.
Custom 3D-printed mounts rigidly couple the head tracker to a GoPro HERO13 with Media Mod and attach the others to the glove dorsum and lateral ankles, with straps for added fixation.
Two interchangeable glove configurations share this layout: MANUS Metagloves measure finger articulation, while Wuji gloves additionally record tactile signals.

blocks.en: 3.2 Whole-Body Reconstruction from Sparse Measurement

blocks.en:
𝐂 3 \mathbf{C}^{3} : Calibrate-Complete-Constrain. Whole-body reconstruction calls for inferring the body joint motion from the rig’s sparse tracker poses.
Yet, coupled ambiguities arise: tracker poses depend jointly on body articulation and rigid attachment to anatomical anchors ( i.e. , head, wrists, and ankle joint frames), allowing mounting errors to be absorbed into estimated motion.
Even calibrated anchors leave intermediate joints undetermined.
We address these with C 3 \mathrm{C}^{3} (Calibrate-Complete-Constrain; Fig. 2 ), separating fixed body-sensor geometry from time-varying motion. Protocol-guided calibration aligns a prescribed movement sequence ( i.e. , the calibration protocol) with a reference motion library by phase.
Robust fitting estimates body shape, scale, and sensor-to-anchor transforms from these correspondences once per mounting configuration. Prior-guided motion completion uses a temporal motion prior, a model for completing unobserved articulation, to generate a motion proposal: an initial whole-body trajectory from anchors. Layered constraints then jointly refine skeletal measurement agreement, surface clearance, and ground non-penetration.
We fuse glove-measured finger articulation and touch as direct interaction evidence.

blocks.en: Protocols. To disentangle body proportions, sensor offsets, and world-frame alignment, we use a calibration protocol comprising standing, A- and T-poses, forward arm extension, head and wrist rotations, elbow flexion, shallow squats, leg raises, and ankle motion. A reference motion library provides consistent anatomical targets without requiring an exact match to the participant’s motion. To accommodate differences in execution speed, we automatically match ordered holds and motion peaks in recorded tracker signals to reference actions, pairing observed device poses with corresponding reference joint poses. The library is cached and reused, limiting participant-specific work to protocol recording and profile fitting. The full protocol and sample-selection rules are detailed in Sec. C.1 .

simulation ( Fig. 6 ).

tracking; protocols are detailed in Secs. F.6 and F.9 .

blocks.en: 6 Conclusion
blocks.zh: 6 结论

blocks.en:
This paper introduces EgoExplorer , an egocentric dataset aligning whole-body motion, hand articulation, contact, and descriptions for human loco-manipulation.
The proposed C 3 \mathrm{C}^{3} pipeline recovers metric body motion from sparse wearable sensing through calibration, temporal completion, and layered constraints.
Evaluations show the benefits of direct sensing, and support this portable approach to capturing and studying coordinated movement and manipulation.

本文介绍EgoExplorer, 一个以自我为中心的数据集, 调整全身运动, 手语表达,接触,和描述 人类的机能操纵。
拟议的C 3\mathrm{C}^{3}管道通过校准、时间完成和分层限制,从稀少的可穿戴感知中恢复了测量体运动。
评价显示直接感知的好处,并支持这种可移植的捕捉和研究协调移动和操纵的方法。

blocks.en: Limitations. Reconstruction cannot guarantee exact recovery of all joints, while tactile sensing has variable reliability. Preliminary studies leave benefits for real-world humanoid learning unverified.

Tactile processing. Wearable tactile response weakens with use and depends on wearing tension
and channel health. Raw amplitude therefore cannot by itself distinguish
light contact from reduced sensitivity or missing data. The three interfaces
in Tab. 10 retain native values (L0), baseline-relative
changes (L1), and 17-region contact with separate health/validity (L2).
Unresponsive taxels are excluded from regional support; insufficient support
makes a region unavailable, not negative. Baselines, response normalization,
and region mappings accompany each recording. These are contact indicators,
not calibrated force or pressure measurements.

blocks.en: Contact is temporally associated with motion, not used to constrain body IK. To preserve brief touches on the 30,Hz grid, each region’s output is the logical OR of valid native-rate detections within the 1/30,s bin centered on the output timestamp. procedure and the operations you may see; the recording may cover only a
subset of them. 1. Preparation. Reagents, catalysts, vessels, and consumables are
retrieved from storage, brought to the bench, and arranged by use. A balance
may be tared before solids are weighed and transferred; pipettes may be
rinsed before liquid handling. 2. Reaction setup. Materials are added to a reaction flask. The
example procedure describes adding solvent, solid substrate, liquid
reagent, and catalyst in sequence, followed by adjustment of heating and
stirring and observation of the apparatus. 3. Monitoring. TLC involves sampling, spotting a plate, and UV
inspection. HPLC sample preparation can involve liquid transfer, dilution,
mixing, filtration into a sample vial, and labeling. 4. Workup. The reaction vessel may be moved from the stirring station
to the fume hood. Subsequent operations include handling the receiving
vessel, pouring, adjusting controls, and inspecting relevant readouts. 5. Extraction. A mixture is transferred into a separatory funnel and
allowed to separate into layers. The stopcock is opened to drain a layer
into a receiver and closed to stop drainage; the other layer is collected
separately. Addition of extraction solvent, mixing, settling, and separation
may be repeated. 6. Rotary evaporation. The flask is connected to the evaporator,
controls are adjusted, and concentration is monitored. Later operations
include stopping the apparatus, releasing vacuum, removing the flask,
and weighing it. 7. Column chromatography. Sample and silica are mixed, material is
loaded into a column, the column and tubing are installed, and the apparatus
is operated to collect fractions. Annotation instructions. Use this background to identify equipment
and interpret the stage of the experiment. Follow the video when deciding
which operations occurred and where their boundaries lie. Preserve visible
relocation, repetition, and correction. Describe the action and its target
concretely, such as “attaches the flask to the rotary evaporator.” Do not
insert steps solely because they appear in the procedure. Leave unreadable
quantities, uncertain identities, and unobserved outcomes unspecified. Output. Return a time-ordered list of segments with start_time , end_time (source-video seconds), skill , description , object_roles , and observed_outcome . Use a short operation label for skill and null for an outcome that cannot be established from the video.

explain the full residual, and the current body mapping and IK trade-offs
leave substantial articulation error.
For the control policy, wrist and foot position rewards use exp ( − e 2 ¯ / 0.3 2 ) \exp(-\overline{e^{2}}/0.3^{2}) , with distances measured in meters. A 5 cm
deviation therefore yields a reward of approximately 0.97. The joint-position
reward has weight 0.1, and no dedicated elbow- or knee-position rewards are
used. These choices provide limited incentives for centimeter-level
precision, and their individual effects have not been isolated by ablation.
The results therefore demonstrate preliminary simulated motion transfer
rather than precise object interaction. Joint optimization of ground contact
and body targets, together with tighter tracking rewards, remains an

blocks.en:
Deployment and sensing. Multi-view RGB reconstruction provides an affordable route to whole-body
capture within a calibrated volume. FreeMoCap supports ordinary USB cameras
and recommends three to four views for general motion capture. Such arrays require overlapping views,
synchronization, and intrinsic/extrinsic calibration; moving the cameras
requires renewed calibration.
Multi-view methods can also recover hands, although occlusion and the small
image scale of fingers make fine articulation challenging ( Zhang et al., 2021 ) . Direct glove sensing complements body capture
and can additionally provide measured contact. Hybrid systems such as
ParaHome combine cameras, an inertial suit, and gloves ( Kim et al., 2025 ) ; HOT3D uses optical markers for hands and objects ( Banerjee et al., 2025 ) ; Nymeria combines an inertial body suit with
wearable Aria devices ( Ma et al., 2024 ) .
Our rig avoids external camera-array and base-station setup and reuses its
body–sensor calibration while mounts remain fixed. Its inside-out trackers
still depend on suitable visual conditions.
